title: the birth of the cousins
hook: the cousins grow up under one roof, and a rivalry is born with them

segments.voice: Yesterday in the birth of the cousins, Kunti's mantra called Dharma, Vayu and Indra, and Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna were born — justice, strength, and skill. Did you tell a younger person what you see growing in them? Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

A fruit tree in a royal garden, and a crowd of boys up in its branches, reaching for fruit. Down below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He puts his foot against the trunk and kicks. The tree shakes, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit. In the water he grabs his cousins and holds them under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget. Today the birth of the cousins ends with one more birth: a grudge.
screen: `A TREE FULL OF COUSINS.` → `BHIMA KICKS THE TRUNK.` → `DURYODHANA DOESN'T FORGET.`

segments.voice: The story moves quickly now. Madri, with Kunti's help, has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest. And in the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five sons of Pandu to Hastinapura, and the two families of cousins now live in one palace. They study, eat and play together. And in the text, play is where the trouble starts. Bhima is stronger than all of them, and he never lets them forget it. Duryodhana watches, and the story says jealousy takes hold of him. So he makes a plan. He arranges a day of water sports by the Ganga, with pavilions and food. Into Bhima's food goes poison. When Bhima, worn out and heavy, lies down by the river, Duryodhana binds him and pushes him into the water. Bhima sinks, down and down, into the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. The snakes bite him, and in the story their venom works against the poison. The Naga king receives him, and Bhima is given a drink that makes him stronger still. Back in Hastinapura, the brothers come home without him. Kunti is frantic, and she says aloud what she suspects. Vidura, the wise uncle, tells her to keep quiet: if she accuses Duryodhana openly, he may turn on her other sons. Then Bhima walks home, alive and stronger, and tells his brothers everything. Yudhishthira's answer is to say nothing for now, and to guard one another. So that's where these six days of births leave us. The cousins were born in one family. Now something else has been born between them, and the brothers have learned to keep their eyes open.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE PALACE.` · `POISON AT THE RIVER.` · `RESCUED AMONG THE NAGAS.` · `KEEP QUIET, AND KEEP WATCH.` · then, large: `A GRUDGE IS BORN TOO.`

segments.voice: Settle in for two minutes. Let the breath find its own pace. Let a face come back from childhood, someone you grew up beside: a brother, a sister, a cousin, a kid next door. Remember one small moment between you, a game, a fight, a shared meal. Don't judge who was right. Just let the memory come, and hold it lightly. If an old sting is still there, notice where it sits. If there's warmth, let it stay a while. The bell holds the time.
Naga, the serpent people below the waters, whose venom worked against the poison in Bhima's blood and left him stronger still.
Your line: a grudge that started young. Today, if a small resentment starts in you, name it to yourself before it grows. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Hindu families tell the Mahabharata to children a piece at a time, and the boyhood of Bhima and Duryodhana, with the poisoned meal and the serpent realm, is one of the pieces told.

fork.setup: you're Kunti. your son Bhima hasn't come home from the river, and you suspect your nephew. what do you do?
options: accuse Duryodhana openly before the court.
keep quiet, as Vidura advises, and protect your other sons.
take your sons and leave the city that night.
fork.reveal: Vidura warns that an open accusation could put her other sons in danger. she keeps quiet, and Bhima soon walks home alive.

original.note: Sanskrit nāga: a serpent; in the story, the serpent people whose realm lies below the waters.

notes: All paraphrase. Days 722–726 were not on disk when this was written; this day takes the cousins' boyhood (Bhima's play, the poisoning, the Naga realm) as the close of the arc. If an earlier day already told the poisoning, this day needs a new angle.
Confirm in Ganguli: Bhima's rough play (shaking boys from trees, ducking them in water, dragging them) and the text's statement that it was without malice.

Confirm: Duryodhana binds the sleeping Bhima and throws him into the Ganga; the snakes' venom counters the poison; the Naga king (Vasuki, with Aryaka) gives him a strength-giving drink. Numbers in the source (bowls drunk, days slept, strength of elephants) are deliberately left out.
Confirm Vidura's counsel to Kunti to keep silent, and Yudhishthira's advice to his brothers to say nothing and guard one another.
howItsDone describes family storytelling in general terms; a Keeper may prefer a specific custom.
